title.narrative: Addressing long-term impacts of the Kakhovka Dam destruction on water resources

description.narrative:
The collapse of the Nova Kakhova dam, on 6 June 2023, only came to aggravate an already catastrophic scenario: hundreds of Ukrainians were rescued from their rooftops as the water released from the breached dam has submerged villages, fields and roads in the southern region of Kherson - the dam’s reservoir holds 18 cubic kilometres and around 600 square kilometres were flooded, as per the region’s governor estimates. The breach led to extensive flooding, impacting 80 settlements across four oblasts: Kherson, Mykolaiv, Dnipropetrovsk, and Zaporizhzhia. Approximately 100,000 residents were directly affected by the resulting deluge. The destruction of the dam also disrupted critical aspects of life in southern Ukraine, including energy production, access to drinking water, irrigation, and river transport. It left a trail of damage in housing, infrastructure, the environment, and cultural heritage.
In this context, UNESCO seeks to mobilize its expertise, networks and resources to support an increased understanding of Dnipro River hydrological dynamics and identify the best management practices that can mitigate the water scarcity scenarios foreseen. In parallel with the actions developed in the scope of culture and education mentioned above, UNESCO has unique expertise in water science to help relieve the long-term impacts of the dam’s destruction.
The project aims to develop a rapid water security assessment, including a mapping of local water resources, and assess the long-term impacts of Kakhovka Dam destruction in freshwater systems and ecosystems. Further, the project aims to identify potential adaptation actions through the tailored application of UNESCO’s acknowledged Climate Risk Informed Decision Analysis (CRIDA) .
